youtube.title: Python pip and venv for Beginners | Python Programming EP 58
youtube.description: In this episode you will install a package with pip, make an isolated environment with venv and know when a package is in the wrong environment, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Packages and environments · 0:53 Is a package installed? · 1:33 One kitchen per recipe · 2:07 Second program · 3:07 Recap · 3:39 Bug of the Day · 4:27 Challenge · 4:47 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "PIP + VENV" in tomato on peach; Xecxec carrying a package box labelled pip install into a clean glass room labelled venv; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec carrying a package box labelled pip install into a clean glass room labelled venv

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Python has a huge library of packages written by other people. Today we learn how to install them safely.

scenes.onScreen: "Packages and environments": three numbered lines (1. pip installs packages from the Python Package Index; 2. A virtual environment is a private folder of packages; 3. Activate the environment before you install) and an analogy card: a kitchen per recipe: each dish gets its own set of ingredients, so one recipe cannot spoil another
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Pip is the tool that installs packages. Pip install, and the package name. But if you install everything into one place, projects start to clash. A virtual environment is a private folder of packages, one per project. Think of a separate kitchen for each recipe. One recipe cannot spoil another. You make one with python dash m venv. You activate it, and then pip installs into it.

scenes.onScreen: pipcheck.py: try to import a package that is not installed yet
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A try block. [HL 2] We try to import a package called pyfiglet. [HL 3] If it works, we say so. [HL 4] If Python cannot find it, [HL 5] we say it is missing. On a fresh computer, the answer is missing. After pip install pyfiglet, the same program says installed. The terminal commands are shown on screen.

scenes.onScreen: Two project boxes, each with its own packages folder; a global Python sits outside both
scenes.animation: Two project boxes with separate package shelves; a global Python box stays unchanged
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. Python sits in the middle. Project one has its own private folder of packages. Project two has another. They can even use different versions of the same package, without clashing. A virtual environment is just that private folder, plus a small script that points Python at it. Activate it, and every pip install goes inside.

scenes.onScreen: inenv.py: compare prefix and base prefix
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] The sys module knows how Python was started. [HL 2] Prefix is where this Python lives. Base prefix is the main installation. Inside a virtual environment, they differ, and this prints True. Outside one, they are the same, and it prints False. Run it before and after you activate your environment, and watch the answer change.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as inenv dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, inenv dot py. False, outside a virtual environment. After you activate one, it prints True.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: pip installs packages into the Python that runs it. Two: A virtual environment is a private set of packages for one project. Three: Activate the environment before you run pip install. Four: Use python -m pip, so pip matches your python. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: the package went to the wrong environment
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We installed the package, but our script says, module not found error, no module named pyfiglet. The package went to a different Python, or a different environment, than the one running our script. Activate your virtual environment, and install with python dash m pip, so pip belongs to the same Python.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the package love virtual environments? It finally had its own room.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the package love virtual environments? It finally had its own room.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: make and use a venv
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge. Create a virtual environment called .venv, activate it, and run python -m pip list. Comment your answer below.

    import pyfiglet

bug.why: pip may have installed the package into a different Python, or a different environment, than the one running your script; python -m pip installs into the Python you run.

shorts.title: What is pip?
shorts.script: Pip is Python's package installer. Pip install, and the name of a package, downloads it from the Python Package Index. Then you can import it. There are hundreds of thousands of packages, for web apps, data, games, and more. Use python dash m pip, so that pip belongs to the same Python that runs your code. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Install a package.

shorts.title: Why venv?
shorts.hook: "If you install every package into one place, projects start to clash, because they need different versions."
shorts.script: If you install every package into one place, projects start to clash, because they need different versions. A virtual environment solves this. It is a private folder of packages, one for each project. Think of a separate kitchen for each recipe. One recipe cannot spoil another. Make one for every project. Then you avoid many problems. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A kitchen per recipe.

shorts.title: Make and activate
shorts.script: Making an environment takes one command. Python dash m venv dot venv. That creates a folder called dot venv. Activate it with the activate script, which is different on Windows and on Mac or Linux. Your terminal prompt changes, to show the environment name. Now every pip install goes into that folder, and nowhere else. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Two commands.

shorts.title: Wrong environment
shorts.script: A common bug. You install a package, but your script says, module not found error. The package went into a different Python than the one running the script. Check which environment is active. Activate the right one, and install with python dash m pip. Then the package and the script share the same Python. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Same Python, same pip.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the package love virtual environments?"
shorts.script: Why did the package love virtual environments? It finally had its own room. Your challenge. Create a virtual environment called dot venv. Activate it. Then run python dash m pip list, and see how short the list is. A fresh environment is nearly empty. Share what you see in the comments, and tell us which system you use. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 58.
